subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: If xʸ = yˣ, show that dy/dx = y(x log y − y)/(x(y log x − x)).

mark_split.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say what you do to both sides first, and what happens to dy/dx after that.

steps.label: Take logarithms of both sides
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Both sides have a variable base and a variable power, so both sides need the logarithm. The rule log(aᵐ) = m log a is what brings each power down in front.
steps.memory_tip: The power always comes down and stands in front of the logarithm: xʸ gives y log x, and yˣ gives x log y.
lines: Here x and y each stand in a base and in a power, so neither the power rule nor the exponential rule applies. Take logarithms of both sides.
∴ y log x = x log y      …(1)
This needs x > 0 and y > 0, so that log x and log y exist.

recall.must_convey: That logarithms are taken on both sides, giving y log x = x log y.
accept: take log on both sides to get y log x equals x log y
the powers come down in front of the logarithms
log of x to the power y is y log x
both sides have variable base and variable power so use logs
rendu vaipulaki log teesukunte y log x equals x log y
apply log a to the m equals m log a on both sides

steps.why: A logarithm turns each power into a product, and a product can be differentiated by the product rule. Without this step neither side of the equation can be differentiated at all.
common_mistakes: Writing log(xʸ) = (log x)ʸ, which keeps the power where it was.
Taking the logarithm of only one side of the equation.

steps.label: Differentiate both sides with respect to x
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Each side is a product of two factors, and y is a function of x, so every derivative of y carries a dy/dx with it. Four terms should appear, two on each side.
steps.memory_tip: y is not a constant. Every time y is differentiated, a dy/dx is written beside it.
lines: Differentiating (1) with respect to x, using the product rule on each side,
y · (1/x) + log x · (dy/dx) = x · (1/y)(dy/dx) + log y · 1

recall.must_convey: That both sides are differentiated by the product rule, with a dy/dx attached to every derivative of y.
accept: use the product rule on both sides
y by x plus log x into dy by dx equals x by y into dy by dx plus log y
every time you differentiate y you write dy by dx
implicit differentiation because y depends on x
y ni differentiate cheste dy by dx kooda rayali
four terms come out, two on each side

steps.why: y is a function of x, not a constant, so differentiating log y gives (1/y)(dy/dx) and differentiating y gives dy/dx. That is what makes this an implicit problem as well as a logarithmic one.
common_mistakes: Treating y as a constant, so that (dy/dx) never appears on the right side.
Differentiating log y as 1/y and leaving out the dy/dx factor.

steps.label: Collect the dy/dx terms
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Move both dy/dx terms to the left and both plain terms to the right, then take dy/dx outside a bracket. Nothing is cancelled here, only rearranged.
steps.memory_tip: All the dy/dx terms go to one side and everything else to the other, exactly as with an ordinary linear equation in one unknown.
lines: From (2), bringing the dy/dx terms to the left and the rest to the right,

recall.must_convey: That the dy/dx terms are gathered on one side and dy/dx is taken outside a bracket.
accept: shift the dy by dx terms to one side and the others to the other side
take dy by dx common outside a bracket
log x minus x by y multiplies dy by dx
the right side becomes log y minus y by x
dy by dx terms okka vaipuki teesukoni common teeyali
treat dy by dx as the unknown and collect it

steps.why: The equation is linear in dy/dx, so gathering its two terms and factoring it out is the only move needed to make it the subject.
common_mistakes: Changing a sign while shifting a term across the equals sign.
Taking dy/dx outside but leaving one of its terms behind on the right.

steps.label: Clear the fractions and finish
steps.margin_note: The last two marks. Write each side over a single denominator first: the left bracket over y, the right side over x. Dividing then gives the printed form directly.
steps.memory_tip: The y that was under the bracket on the left ends up on top of the answer, and the x that was under the right side ends up on the bottom.
lines: Writing each side over a single denominator,
log x − (x/y) = (y log x − x)/y     and     log y − (y/x) = (x log y − y)/x
So (3) becomes  (dy/dx) · (y log x − x)/y = (x log y − y)/x
∴ dy/dx = [(x log y − y)/x] · [y/(y log x − x)]

lines.text: ∴ dy/dx = y(x log y − y) / (x(y log x − x))

recall.must_convey: That each side is put over a single denominator and the division gives dy/dx = y(x log y − y)/(x(y log x − x)).
accept: put both sides over a common denominator and divide
the left bracket becomes y log x minus x over y
the right side becomes x log y minus y over x
y comes to the top and x goes to the bottom
common denominator teesukunte printed form vasthundi
dy by dx equals y into x log y minus y over x into y log x minus x

steps.why: The question states the answer, so the marks are for landing on that exact form. Clearing the small fractions x/y and y/x is what turns the rearranged equation into the printed expression, with y on top and x on the bottom.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as (log y − y/x)/(log x − x/y), which is correct but is not the form asked for.
Exchanging x and y in the final line, which reverses the whole fraction.
